title: Why dusk drains the color
question: Why do colors fade as the light dims?
hook: A red car in daylight turns gray at night, and your eyes are the reason.
idea: Color comes from cones that need bright light, so when only rods are working the world loses its hues.

beats.prompt: You step from a sunny street into a very dim cellar. After a few minutes your eyes adjust, but the room looks nearly colorless. Why?

choices.label: Rods take over, and they play little part in color
The objects themselves lose their hues in the dark
choices.feedback: It tempts because the objects look different, but the light and your receptors changed, not the things.

choices.label: Cones grow stronger and wash out every hue
choices.feedback: It sounds plausible, but cones are the cells that need bright light to carry color.

beats.explain: In very dim light, rod cells detect the light and they play little if any role in color vision. Cones, which handle color, work in brighter light.

beats.prompt: match each situation to the cells doing the seeing
beats.explain: Cones work in daylight and give color, rods work in very dim light, and in between both send signals.

beats.prompt: sort each color by how it is made
beats.explain: Spectral colors come from a narrow band of wavelengths, while pink, brown and navy come from mixing spectral colors with white, gray or black.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about the eye is wrong. Which?
steps: Humans have three cone types, labeled short, medium and long.
The labels come from where each type's sensitivity peaks.
So the long cones must be the red detectors, medium green and short blue.
That makes RGB a handy way to describe color on a screen.
beats.explain: The long cones peak in the greenish-yellow, so the cone types do not match red, green and blue. RGB is convenient but is not based directly on the cones.
